approved: Social Services and Other Legislation Amendment (Simplifying Income Reporting and Other Measures) Bill 2020
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would change how employment income is assessed for social security payments, using actual paid amounts instead of estimates.
Services Australia would use data from the Australian Taxation Office's Single Touch Payroll system to determine a person's rate of payment.
The bill would commence on 1 July 2020 if it receives Royal Assent before 15 May 2020, or on the first day of the first calendar month after two months from Royal Assent otherwise.
Amends the Social Security Act 1991 to assess employment income once it is paid to a recipient.
Amends the Social Security (Administration) Act 1999 to allow Services Australia to use Single Touch Payroll data.
Amends the A New Tax System (Family Assistance) (Administration) Act 1999 and the Student Assistance Act 1973 for the same purpose.
Amends provisions regarding the work bonus and pension bonus scheme.
Social security recipients who report employment income.

The speaker moved an amendment criticising the government's three-year defence of the failed Robodebt program and repeated attempts to cut pensions and social security, while supporting the bill's shift to income reporting when paid and use of Single Touch Payroll data to improve accuracy. The speaker also argued the government cannot be trusted due to past pension cuts, increased pension age proposals, and a bill to double the liquid assets waiting period for Newstart, which would force vulnerable Australians to wait up to six months for support.

The speaker supported the Social Services and Other Legislation Amendment (Simplifying Income Reporting and Other Measures) Bill 2020, which allows 1.2 million welfare recipients to report earnings as they appear on payslips using Single Touch Payroll, with no rate changes and projected annual savings of $650 million. The speaker also noted the government reduced welfare dependency to 13.5%—the lowest in 30 years—and created 1.4 million jobs since 2013.

The speaker supported the Social Services and Other Legislation Amendment (Simplifying Income Reporting and Other Measures) Bill 2020 but criticised the government's track record with digital projects, citing failures like My Health Record ($2 billion), the 2016 census outage ($30 million cost blowout), and the 2019 myGov outage. They also condemned the robodebt scheme, noting nearly 2,000 people died after receiving notices, money was taken from 73 estates of deceased individuals, and internal documents revealed the government lacked legal authority to issue the debts.

The member argued for the Social Services and Other Legislation Amendment (Simplifying Income Reporting and Other Measures) Bill 2020, which will change employment income reporting to Centrelink from when earned to when paid, aligning with Single Touch Payroll, and claimed it will simplify reporting, reduce overpayments, and save $2.1 billion over four years, while criticising Labor for politicising the issue.

The speaker supported the Social Services and Other Legislation Amendment (Simplifying Income Reporting and Other Measures) Bill and the shadow minister's second reading amendment, citing a news.com.au survey showing 28% of Australians on "Struggle Street" and 14% "barely coping" due to low wages and inadequate welfare payments. They criticised the government for not increasing Newstart, highlighted ongoing robodebt issues including incorrect debts and 73 deceased estates affected, and called for the government to admit mistakes and repay victims.

The speaker supported the bill's income reporting changes but criticised the government's record on Centrelink digitisation, citing the robodebt scheme, and argued that Newstart’s $559 per fortnight and its income test thresholds ($104 and $254) are inadequate, calling for a payment increase and refund of algorithm-based debts.

The Social Services and Other Legislation Amendment (Simplifying Income Reporting and Other Measures) Bill 2020 was characterized as an attempt to fix the robodebt failure, with a commitment to closely monitor its implementation. The critique cited that 80 per cent of constituents with robodebt issues had debts dropped or refunded, and cited historical Coalition pension cuts, including a 2014 $80 weekly cut, a 2015 assets-test change affecting 370,000 pensioners, and a 2016 proposal for 190,000 pensioners limiting overseas travel to six weeks.

The speaker argued that the bill addresses the government’s illegal robodebt scheme, which used faulty data to wrongly demand repayments from welfare recipients, and noted that thousands of victims still face legal battles despite partial government acknowledgment of wrongdoing.
